results.content: # Title:Scale-aware Adaptive Supervised Network with Limited Medical Annotations. View a PDF of the paper titled Scale-aware Adaptive Supervised Network with Limited Medical Annotations, by Zihan Li and 4 other authors. > Abstract:Medical image segmentation faces critical challenges in semi-supervised learning scenarios due to severe annotation scarcity requiring expert radiological knowledge, significant inter-annotator variability across different viewpoints and expertise levels, and inadequate multi-scale feature integration for precise boundary delineation in complex anatomical structures. To address these fundamental challenges, we propose SASNet (Scale-aware Adaptive Supervised Network), a dual-branch architecture that leverages both low-level and high-level feature representations through novel scale-aware adaptive reweight mechanisms. | Subjects: | Image and Video Processing (eess.IV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) |. | Cite as: | arXiv:2601.01005 [eess.IV] |. |  | (or  arXiv:2601.01005v1 [eess.IV] for this version) |. results.content: Optical detection methods for label-free imaging and sensing are typically based on internal contrast mechanisms of the sample; for example, its ability to delay the light interacting with the sample due to refractive index changes, or its ability to create unique optical spectroscopic, auto-fluorescence, and birefringence or acoustic signatures. We present dynamic spectrally encoded confocal microscopy (D-SECM), a high-speed, label-free imaging technique for real-time visualization of subcellular metabolic activity. Multispectral imaging (MSI) enables label-free analysis of biological tissues by capturing images across multiple wavelengths, enhancing contrast and biochemical specificity over traditional brightfield microscopy. In contrast, label-free optical imaging enables non-invasive access to phenotypic traits of living cells, keeping them viable and sterile for downstream use. We present a label-free, preparation-free approach to blood-cell imaging based on near-focus interference (NFI) quantitative phase imaging, designed for both pre-clinical and clinical use. Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) based on digital holographic microscopy (DHM), can be combined with microscopes and provides label-free access of biophysical cell properties and morphology.
